blocks.html: In Punnett Squares you used letters for alleles. Those letters began with one patient experimenter. In the 1850s and 1860s Gregor Mendel, a friar in Brno (now in the Czech Republic), grew thousands of pea plants and counted their traits. He reported his results in 1865 and published them in 1866.

Mendel started with true-breeding plants: plants that, pollinated by themselves, always gave offspring like themselves. He crossed two true-breeding parents that differed in one trait, such as round seeds and wrinkled seeds. That is the P generation. Their offspring are the F1, and the offspring of F1 plants pollinated by themselves are the F2.

Every F1 plant showed only one form of the trait, the dominant one. In the F2, the hidden recessive form came back in about one plant in four: a 3:1 ratio. Each plant carries two copies of each "factor" (gene), and the two copies separate when gametes form (the law of segregation).

blocks.html: Why 3:1? Call the round allele R and the wrinkled allele r. The F1 are all Rr. Each F1 parent puts R into half of its gametes and r into the other half. Two gametes join at random, so the chances are RR ¼, Rr ½ and rr ¼. Only rr looks wrinkled, so ¾ of the F2 are round and ¼ wrinkled.

¼ of 400 is 100.

blocks.title: Reading real counts
blocks.q: Mendel's stem-length F2 had 787 tall and 277 short plants. Is that close to 3:1?
steps: Chance makes real counts wobble around the expected ratio, the way 100 coin flips rarely give exactly 50 heads.

blocks.html: People often think the recessive trait was destroyed in the F1, or that the parents' traits blend. If they blended, the F1 would be in between and the F2 could never show pure white again. The white allele was hidden, not lost: it reappears in about a quarter of the F2.

blocks.html: A monohybrid cross follows one gene. You already know the steps from Mendel's Experiments. Here we make them exact, so you can predict any one-gene cross.

items: Write each parent's genotype (for example Aa).
Write the gametes: each gamete gets one allele of the gene. Aa makes A and a; AA makes only A.
Fill the Punnett square: each box joins one gamete from the side with one from the top.
Count genotypes (AA, Aa, aa), then count phenotypes (what the organism looks like).

blocks.html: For Aa × Aa the genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and the phenotype ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive, because AA and Aa look the same.

Each box of the square is equally likely, because each gamete type is made equally often and gametes join at random. So a box is a probability: in a 4-box square, each box is ¼. Counting boxes is the same as adding probabilities.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Fill each box: one allele from the top, one from the side. Then press Check.

blocks.title: A cross with a heterozygote
blocks.q: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to brown (b). Cross Bb × bb. Give the genotype and phenotype ratios.
steps: Gametes: Bb gives B and b; bb gives only b.
Boxes: Bb, Bb, bb, bb.
Genotypes: 2 Bb : 2 bb, which is 1 : 1.
Phenotypes: 2 black : 2 brown, which is 1 : 1.
blocks.a: Genotypes 1 Bb : 1 bb; phenotypes 1 black : 1 brown.

blocks.title: Two ratios from one square
blocks.q: Cross Tt × Tt (tall is dominant). What fraction are tall, and what fraction are Tt?
steps: Boxes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Tall: TT and Tt, so 3 of 4 boxes: ¾.
Tt alone: 2 of 4 boxes: ½.

head: Cross
Genotype ratio
Phenotype ratio
blocks.cap: The four crosses worth knowing by heart.

blocks.html: Two slips are common. One is giving the genotype ratio (1:2:1) when the question asks for the phenotype ratio (3:1). The other is counting AA and Aa as different looks. Check: a phenotype ratio for one gene with complete dominance has at most two parts.

blocks.html: A purple pea plant could be PP or Pp. Both look the same, so looking will not tell you. In Monohybrid Crosses we went from genotypes to offspring. A test cross runs that idea backward: from offspring to a hidden genotype.

Cross the unknown dominant-looking organism with a homozygous recessive (pp) one. If any offspring show the recessive trait, the unknown was Pp. If many offspring all show the dominant trait, the unknown is almost surely PP.

The pp parent can give only p, so it never hides anything: each offspring shows whatever allele came from the unknown parent. A PP parent gives only P, so every offspring is Pp and purple. A Pp parent gives p half the time, so about half the offspring are pp and white.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: If the unknown is Pp, half the boxes are white.

blocks.title: Reading a result
blocks.q: A black guinea pig (black is dominant) is crossed with a brown one. The litter has 3 black and 2 brown pups. What is the black parent's genotype?
steps: The brown parent is bb and gives only b.
A brown pup is bb, so it got b from the black parent too.
So the black parent carries b.

blocks.title: How sure can we be?
blocks.q: A Pp plant is test-crossed and gives 5 offspring. What is the chance that all 5 are purple just by luck?
steps: Each offspring of Pp × pp is purple with chance ½.
Offspring are independent, so multiply: ½ × ½ × ½ × ½ × ½.

blocks.html: Two errors. First, crossing the unknown with a dominant-looking organism: a PP partner hides the result, because every offspring gets a P from it. Second, deciding "PP" from only two or three purple offspring. A Pp plant gives all-purple small litters fairly often; more offspring make the answer more certain.
One recessive offspring settles it: the unknown is heterozygous. All-dominant offspring never prove PP; they only make Pp less and less likely.

sources.name: OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 8.2 Laws of Inheritance (test cross)

blocks.html: A Punnett square is a picture of probability. For bigger questions, such as three genes at once or several children in a row, drawing squares gets slow. Two rules from Compound Probability do the work faster.
Product rule: for independent events, the chance that both happen is the product. Sum rule: for outcomes that cannot happen together, the chance of one or the other is the sum.

Genes on different chromosomes sort independently in meiosis (see How Meiosis Makes Variation), so what one gene does tells you nothing about another. That is what "independent" means, and it is why you can multiply. A child who is AA cannot also be Aa, so those outcomes are separate and you can add them.

blocks.title: The product rule
blocks.q: Parents are AaBb × AaBb, with genes on different chromosomes. What is the chance of an aabb child?
steps: Gene A alone: Aa × Aa gives aa with chance ¼.
Gene B alone: Bb × Bb gives bb with chance ¼.
Both: ¼ × ¼.

blocks.title: The sum rule
blocks.q: From Aa × Aa, what is the chance the offspring is heterozygous?
steps: Aa can happen two ways: A from the first parent and a from the second, or a first and A second.
Each way has chance ½ × ½ = ¼.
Add them: ¼ + ¼.

blocks.title: Both rules together
blocks.q: AaBbCc × AaBbCc. What is the chance of an offspring that shows the dominant A trait, is bb, and shows the dominant C trait?
steps: Dominant A: ¾ (AA or Aa, sum rule: ¼ + ½).
bb: ¼.
Dominant C: ¾.
Multiply: ¾ × ¼ × ¾ = 9/64.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: One gene at a time: each box is ¼. The 16-box square for two genes is these squares multiplied.

blocks.html: Two common errors. Adding when you should multiply: the chance of aa and bb is not ¼ + ¼ = ½; that would make a rare combination common. And the "due" error: if two Aa parents already have three children with the dominant trait, the chance the next one is aa is still ¼. Each child is a new, independent event; the alleles have no memory.
Quick check: a product of chances is never bigger than either chance, and a sum of separate outcomes is never more than 1.

blocks.html: Mendel also followed two traits at once, such as seed shape (R round, r wrinkled) and seed color (Y yellow, y green). A cross of two RrYy plants is a dihybrid cross. It rests on the product rule and on independent assortment.
A gamete carries one allele of each gene. RrYy makes four kinds of gametes, RY, Ry, rY and ry, in equal numbers. RrYy × RrYy fills a 16-box square with a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio.

Because the genes sort independently, each gene gives its usual 3 : 1. Combine them with the product rule: both dominant ¾ × ¾ = 9/16; dominant shape and green ¾ × ¼ = 3/16; wrinkled and yellow ¼ × ¾ = 3/16; both recessive ¼ × ¼ = 1/16. Those are 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

blocks.title: Writing gametes
blocks.q: List the gametes of AaBb, and of AABb.
steps: Pair each allele of gene A with each allele of gene B, like FOIL.
AaBb: A with B, A with b, a with B, a with b.
AABb: A with B, A with b (both A alleles are the same).
blocks.a: AaBb: AB, Ab, aB, ab. AABb: AB, Ab.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: The same cross with A for round and B for yellow. The 16 boxes, colored by phenotype: 9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow, 1 wrinkled green.

blocks.title: Counting offspring
blocks.q: From RrYy × RrYy, 320 seeds are grown. About how many are wrinkled and yellow?
steps: Wrinkled: ¼. Yellow: ¾.
Wrinkled and yellow: ¼ × ¾ = 3/16.

blocks.title: A test cross with two genes
blocks.q: RrYy × rryy. What is the phenotype ratio?
steps: RrYy makes RY, Ry, rY, ry, each ¼; rryy makes only ry.
Offspring: RrYy, Rryy, rrYy, rryy, each ¼.
blocks.a: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green).

blocks.html: The most common mistake is writing gametes such as Aa or Bb: two alleles of the same gene. Meiosis separates the two alleles of each gene, so a gamete never has both. Check every gamete: it must have exactly one letter for each gene.
The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 rule needs genes on different chromosomes. Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to travel together; that is linkage, a topic for later study.

blocks.html: In Mendel's peas one allele fully hid the other. Many genes do not work that way. In monohybrid crosses the heterozygote looked like the dominant parent; here it looks different.

Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between. Red (RR) × white (rr) snapdragons give pink (Rr). Codominance: both alleles show fully, side by side. In roan cattle, a heterozygote has a coat of red hairs mixed with white hairs.

An allele usually stands for a version of a protein. In snapdragons, one copy of the red allele makes only about half as much red pigment as two copies, so the flower is pale: pink. In codominance, each allele makes its own working product, so both products show, as in AB blood (see Multiple Alleles: Blood Types).

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: Pink × pink: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The phenotype ratio matches the genotype ratio.

blocks.title: Pink × pink
blocks.q: Two pink snapdragons (Rr) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are red, pink and white?
steps: Boxes: RR, Rr, Rr, rr.
Each genotype has its own color, so count genotypes.
blocks.a: ¼ red, ½ pink, ¼ white.

blocks.title: Pink × white
blocks.q: A pink snapdragon is crossed with a white one. What do the offspring look like?
steps: Rr × rr: gametes R, r and r.
Boxes: Rr, Rr, rr, rr.

blocks.title: Which pattern?
blocks.q: A red-coated bull is crossed with a white-coated cow. The calf's coat has red hairs and white hairs mixed together. Which pattern is this?
steps: The calf is not a single in-between color.
Both parents' colors show at once, each in its own hairs.

blocks.html: Pink flowers can look like proof that traits blend. Test it: cross two pinks. If traits blended, every offspring would be pink forever. Instead red and white come back in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, so the R and r alleles stayed separate the whole time. Only the look of the heterozygote is in between.

OpenStax, Biology 2e, 12.3 Laws of Inheritance (incomplete dominance, codominance)

blocks.html: So far each gene had two alleles. Many genes have more in the population. The gene for the ABO blood types has three: IA, IB and i. It mixes the ideas of codominance and ordinary dominance.
IA and IB are codominant; both are dominant to i. A person has two of the three alleles, which makes six genotypes and four blood types.

I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>B</sup> each code for an enzyme that adds a different sugar marker to the surface of red blood cells. The i allele codes for no working enzyme. One I<sup>A</sup> is enough to add A markers, so I<sup>A</sup>i is type A. With I<sup>A</sup> and I<sup>B</sup>, both markers are added: type AB.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: I<sup>A</sup>i × I<sup>B</sup>i: one box each of AB, A, B and O.

blocks.title: All four types from one couple
blocks.q: A parent with type A blood (I<sup>A</sup>i) and a parent with type B (I<sup>B</sup>i) have children. What blood types are possible?
steps: Gametes: I<sup>A</sup> or i; I<sup>B</sup> or i.
Boxes: I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> (AB), I<sup>A</sup>i (A), I<sup>B</sup>i (B), ii (O).
blocks.a: AB, A, B and O, each with chance ¼.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: Two parents with type A blood have a child with type O. What are the parents' genotypes?
steps: Type O is ii, so the child got i from each parent.
Each parent is type A and carries i.

blocks.title: What cannot happen
blocks.q: Can a parent with type AB blood have a child with type O?
steps: The AB parent is I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> and gives either I<sup>A</sup> or I<sup>B</sup>.
A type O child (ii) needs an i from each parent.

blocks.html: Because three alleles exist, some people think a person can carry all three. Each person has only two copies of the gene, one on each chromosome of the pair. The third allele exists elsewhere in the population, in other people.

sources.name: OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 8.2 Laws of Inheritance (multiple alleles)
OpenStax, Biology 2e, 12.3 Laws of Inheritance (multiple alleles; the ABO blood groups)

blocks.html: Pea seeds are round or wrinkled, with nothing in between. But people are not "tall" or "short"; heights spread over a smooth range. Dihybrid crosses already showed how two genes combine. Add more genes and the steps blur into a curve.
A polygenic trait is shaped by many genes, each adding a little, and usually by the environment too. The result is a continuous range that often forms a bell-shaped curve.

Imagine wheat kernel color set by genes A and B, where each capital allele adds one dose of red pigment. AaBb × AaBb offspring have 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 doses. There are more ways to get 2 doses (AAbb, aaBB and four kinds of AaBb boxes) than 0 or 4, so the middle shades are most common: 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1 out of 16. With three genes there are 7 shades, 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1 out of 64.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.xlabel: Number of capital alleles (doses of red pigment)
opts.title: Three genes: AaBbCc × AaBbCc

blocks.cap: Three genes already give a bell shape. Real traits involve many more genes, and the environment smooths the steps.

blocks.title: Counting classes
blocks.q: Kernel color is set by 4 genes like those above. In a cross of two plants heterozygous for all four, how many color classes appear?
steps: Each offspring has 8 alleles of these genes.
The number of capital alleles can be 0, 1, 2, … 8.

blocks.title: The rare extreme
blocks.q: In AaBb × AaBb (two genes), what fraction of the offspring are the darkest shade?
steps: Darkest means 4 capital alleles: AABB only.
AA has chance ¼ and BB has chance ¼.

blocks.html: The environment matters. Two cuttings of the same plant, which have identical genes, grow to different heights in rich and poor soil. In people, height depends on many genes and also on nutrition and health during childhood. Genes set a range; conditions decide where in the range a person lands.

It is natural to expect every trait to sort into neat boxes, as in Mendel's peas. Most traits do not. Mendel chose traits controlled mostly by one gene. Height, crop yield and the color of wheat kernels involve many genes plus the environment, so they vary smoothly.

blocks.html: In Chromosomes and Their Numbers you met the X and Y chromosomes. XX individuals are female and XY individuals are male. The X carries many genes that have nothing to do with being male or female; the much smaller Y carries few. Genes on the X are called X-linked.

An XX individual has two copies of each X-linked gene; an XY individual has one. So one recessive X-linked allele shows in an XY individual. Write the alleles on the X: XA, Xa. The Y has no allele for these genes.

A son gets his Y from his father, so his only X comes from his mother. A daughter gets one X from each parent. That is why X-linked recessive traits, like red-green color blindness, are much more common in males: one recessive allele is enough. A female needs two, and a female with one is a carrier with normal vision.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: A carrier mother × a father with normal vision.

blocks.title: A carrier mother
blocks.q: X<sup>A</sup>X<sup>a</sup> × X<sup>A</sup>Y (a = color blindness). What are the chances for sons and for daughters?
steps: Mother's gametes: X<sup>A</sup> or X<sup>a</sup>. Father's: X<sup>A</sup> or Y.
Daughters get the father's X<sup>A</sup>: X<sup>A</sup>X<sup>A</sup> or X<sup>A</sup>X<sup>a</sup>. All have normal vision; half are carriers.
Sons get the father's Y: X<sup>A</sup>Y or X<sup>a</sup>Y. Half are color blind.
blocks.a: Daughters: none affected (½ carriers). Sons: ½ color blind.

blocks.title: Two ways to ask
blocks.q: In the same cross, what is the chance that a child is a color-blind son?
steps: Of the four equally likely boxes, only X<sup>a</sup>Y is a color-blind son.
Compare: "the chance a son is color blind" counts only the two son boxes, so it is ½.

blocks.title: A color-blind father
blocks.q: X<sup>A</sup>X<sup>A</sup> × X<sup>a</sup>Y. Can a son be color blind?
steps: Sons get their X from the mother, who has only X<sup>A</sup>.
Daughters get the father's X<sup>a</sup>, so they are all carriers.
blocks.a: No son is color blind; every daughter is a carrier.

blocks.html: Two slips. One is giving the Y chromosome an allele (X<sup>A</sup>Y<sup>a</sup>): the Y has no copy of X-linked genes. The other is thinking an X-linked trait passes from father to son. A father gives his son a Y, never his X, so he cannot pass an X-linked allele to a son.

OpenStax, Biology 2e, 12.3 Laws of Inheritance (sex-linked traits)
Next Generation Science Standards, HS-LS3-1: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

blocks.html: With people we cannot set up crosses, so geneticists read family trees called pedigrees. A square is a male, a circle a female, and a shaded shape means the trait shows. A horizontal line joins two parents; their children hang below. This topic uses test-cross reasoning and X-linked traits.

Look for the telltale pattern. Two unaffected parents with an affected child: the trait is recessive. Two affected parents with an unaffected child: the trait is dominant. A dominant trait does not skip generations: every affected person has an affected parent.

If unaffected parents have an affected child, the child got an allele for the trait from each parent, though neither parent showed it. Only a recessive allele can hide like that, so both parents are carriers (Aa). If two affected parents have an unaffected child, each parent carried a hidden "normal" allele. A hidden allele in an affected person means the trait's allele is dominant.

blocks.name: bi-pedigree
blocks.cap: Unaffected parents (I-1 and I-2) with an affected son (II-2): a recessive trait.

blocks.title: Naming the pattern
blocks.q: In the pedigree above, is the trait dominant or recessive? What are the parents' genotypes?
steps: II-2 is affected, but neither parent is.
So the allele hid in both parents: recessive.
II-2 is aa and got a from each parent; the parents show the dominant look.

blocks.title: A carrier chance
blocks.q: In the same family, II-1 is unaffected. What is the chance she is a carrier?
steps: Aa × Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa, aa.
She is unaffected, so she is not aa. That leaves AA, Aa, Aa.
2 of those 3 are Aa.

blocks.html: X-linked recessive traits leave their own mark: many more affected males than females, passed from a carrier mother to some of her sons, and never from father to son. Each claim in a pedigree is a test: if a pattern breaks any rule, that pattern is ruled out.

It is tempting to call a trait dominant because many people in the family have it. How often a trait appears does not decide it; the pattern does. A recessive trait can be common in a family, and a dominant one can be rare. Look for the two telltale couples instead.

blocks.html: In Nucleic Acids you met the nucleotide: a sugar, a phosphate and a base. DNA is two long chains of nucleotides wound around each other. Its shape explains both how it stores information and how it is copied.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: The double helix: two sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside, base pairs like the rungs of a twisted ladder.

blocks.html: DNA is a double helix. Sugars and phosphates form each strand's backbone. The bases point inward and pair: A with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three). The two strands run in opposite directions: they are antiparallel, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.

Why only A–T and G–C? A and G are large bases with two rings; T and C are small, with one ring. A large base always pairs with a small one, so the ladder has the same width all along. Of the large-small pairs, only A–T and G–C line up their hydrogen bonds. So each strand fixes the other: if you know one, you know its partner.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: Build the partner strand: tap each box to pick the base that pairs with the one above.

blocks.title: Writing the partner strand
blocks.q: One strand reads 5′-ATGCCA-3′. Write the partner strand lined up under it.
steps: Pair base by base: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G, C→G, A→T.
The partner runs the other way, so label its ends 3′ and 5′.

blocks.title: Chargaff's rule
blocks.q: In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are A. What percent are G?
steps: Every A pairs with a T, so T is also 30%.
A + T = 60%, which leaves 40% for G + C.
G pairs with C, so they are equal: 40% ÷ 2.

blocks.html: The pairing rule came from two lines of evidence. Erwin Chargaff measured the bases in DNA from many species and found that A always matched T and G matched C, though the A amount differed from species to species. X-ray pictures of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin showed a helix. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick put these facts together in the double-helix model.

Two common slips: pairing A with G, and thinking all four bases must be 25%. The rule is A = T and G = C. A and G can be quite different: human DNA has more A–T pairs than G–C pairs. Check your answer: %A + %T + %G + %C must make 100.

sources.name: OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 9.1 The Structure of DNA
OpenStax, Biology 2e, 14.2 DNA Structure and Sequencing
Next Generation Science Standards, HS-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes
Grokipedia, Chargaff's rules

blocks.html: Before a cell divides (see The Cell Cycle), it copies all of its DNA. The pairing rule makes this possible: each strand carries the information to rebuild the other.

In replication, helicase unzips the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases. DNA polymerase then adds matching nucleotides to each old strand, A across from T and G across from C. Each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand: replication is semiconservative.

blocks.name: bi-dna
blocks.cap: Step through: Start, Unzip, Build, Done. Each copy keeps one parent strand (dark) and gets one new strand (light).

blocks.html: Each old strand is a template. Because A can only pair with T and G only with C, there is just one strand that fits each template. So the two copies come out identical to each other and to the original. DNA polymerase also checks its work and fixes most of its own mistakes.

items: Helicase unwinds and unzips the helix.
Primase lays down a short RNA primer, because DNA polymerase can only add to an existing strand.
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the new strand, always building it in the 5′→3′ direction.
DNA ligase seals the gaps between pieces of new DNA.

blocks.title: Building on a template
blocks.q: An old strand reads 3′-TACGGA-5′ after the helix unzips. What new strand is built on it?
steps: Pair each base: T→A, A→T, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→T.
The new strand runs the opposite way.

blocks.title: The Meselson-Stahl experiment
blocks.q: In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen, then moved them to light nitrogen. After one round of copying, all the DNA was of middle weight. Why?
steps: Heavy DNA had two heavy strands.
In semiconservative copying, each new molecule keeps one heavy strand and adds one light strand.
One heavy and one light strand weigh in between.
blocks.a: Every molecule was a hybrid: half old (heavy), half new (light).

blocks.title: Counting after several rounds
blocks.q: One heavy DNA molecule is copied 3 times in light nitrogen. How many of the molecules still contain a heavy strand?
steps: After 3 rounds there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 molecules.
The two original heavy strands are never broken up or lost; each sits in its own molecule.
blocks.a: 2 of the 8 (the other 6 are all light).

blocks.html: A common picture is that the cell builds a brand-new double helix beside the old one, which stays whole (the "conservative" idea). Meselson and Stahl ruled that out: after one round there was no fully heavy DNA left. Each copy keeps one parent strand as its template.

blocks.html: DNA stays in the nucleus, but proteins are built at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. The cell sends a working copy of one gene out as messenger RNA (mRNA). Making that copy is transcription. It uses the same base pairing as DNA, with one change.
RNA polymerase opens a gene and reads its template strand, building a complementary mRNA. RNA has U (uracil) instead of T, so the rules are: DNA A → RNA U, T → A, G → C, C → G.

RNA is a nucleic acid too, but its sugar is ribose and it uses U in place of T. U pairs with A just as T does. Only one strand of the gene, the template, is read. The other strand, the coding strand, has the same sequence as the mRNA, except with T where the mRNA has U.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: Step through the gene: RNA polymerase reads the template 3′→5′ and builds mRNA 5′→3′.

blocks.title: From the template strand
blocks.q: A template strand reads 3′-TACGGATTC-5′. What mRNA is made?
steps: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U, T→A, T→A, C→G.

blocks.title: From the coding strand
blocks.q: A gene's coding strand reads 5′-ATGTTCGGA-3′. What is the mRNA?
steps: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand.
Just swap each T for U.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: An mRNA reads 5′-AUGGCA-3′. What was the template strand?
steps: Each mRNA base paired with a template base: A with T, U with A, G with C, C with G.

blocks.html: In eukaryotes, the new RNA is also processed before it leaves the nucleus: a cap and a tail are added, and stretches called introns are cut out. The finished mRNA then travels through a nuclear pore to the ribosomes, where translation begins.

Two slips are common. One is writing T in the RNA: RNA never has T, so every A on the template becomes U. The other is copying the template letter for letter. The mRNA is complementary to the template; it matches the coding strand. Check: no T anywhere, and each mRNA base pairs with the template base above it.

blocks.html: The mRNA from transcription is a message written in bases. A protein is a chain of amino acids (see Proteins). Translation turns the first language into the second.

The ribosome reads the mRNA three bases at a time. Each three-base word is a codon. A transfer RNA (tRNA) with the matching anticodon brings the right amino acid. The ribosome links the amino acids in order, starting at the start codon AUG and stopping at a stop codon.

Why three bases? With four bases, one-letter words would name only 4 amino acids and two-letter words only 4 × 4 = 16. Three-letter words give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons: enough for 20 amino acids plus start and stop signals. The tRNA is the adapter: one end pairs with the codon, the other end carries the amino acid.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: Step codon by codon. Translation starts at the first AUG, not at the first base.

items: Start: the small ribosome subunit binds the mRNA and finds AUG. A tRNA carrying methionine pairs with it.
Elongation: the next tRNA brings its amino acid; the ribosome joins it to the chain and moves one codon along.
Stop: at UAA, UAG or UGA no tRNA fits; a release factor frees the finished chain, which folds into a protein.

blocks.title: Counting amino acids
blocks.q: An mRNA has AUG, then 99 more bases, then the stop codon UAA. How many amino acids are in the protein?
steps: AUG is a codon and codes for methionine: 1 amino acid.
99 more bases make 99 ÷ 3 = 33 codons, each one amino acid.
The stop codon adds none.

blocks.title: Codon and anticodon
blocks.q: A codon reads 5′-UUC-3′. What is the tRNA anticodon, written 3′→5′ under it?
steps: The anticodon pairs with the codon: U with A, U with A, C with G.

blocks.html: Two misunderstandings are common. One is that each base stands for one amino acid; in fact three bases make one codon. The other is that the tRNA carries a codon. The tRNA carries the anticodon, which pairs with the codon on the mRNA, and it carries the amino acid. Check: the number of amino acids should be the number of codons from AUG up to, not including, the stop.

blocks.html: You know from Translation that each codon names one amino acid. The full dictionary is the genetic code, usually printed as a codon table. Reading it is a skill worth practicing.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: The codon table. Start (AUG) and the three stop codons are marked.

blocks.html: To read a codon, find its first base on the left, its second base across the top, and its third base on the right. Translation starts at AUG (methionine, Met) and ends at UAA, UAG or UGA. There are 64 codons for 20 amino acids.

Because 64 codons share 20 amino acids, most amino acids have more than one codon: leucine has six, glycine four, methionine only one. Codons for the same amino acid usually differ only in the third base. That redundancy protects the protein: many changes in a third base change nothing.

blocks.title: One codon
blocks.q: Which amino acid does the codon GCU code for?
steps: First base G: the bottom row.
Second base C: the second column.
Third base U: the first line in that box.

blocks.title: A whole message
blocks.q: Translate 5′-GGAUGUUUAAAUGA-3′.
steps: Find the first AUG: it starts at the third base. Ignore GG before it.
Read in threes from AUG: AUG UUU AAA UGA.
AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, AAA = Lys, UGA = stop.

blocks.title: From DNA letters
blocks.q: A gene's coding strand has the codon TGG. What amino acid does it code for?
steps: The table uses mRNA letters, so change T to U: UGG.
UGG is tryptophan.

blocks.html: The code is nearly universal: bacteria, plants and people read the same codons as the same amino acids, with only a few small exceptions. That shared code is strong evidence that all life is related, and it is why a bacterium can make a human protein in Recombinant DNA.

Two errors are common: looking up DNA letters (T is not in the table; change T to U first) and starting at the first base of the message instead of at AUG. Find AUG, then read in threes, and stop at the first stop codon.

blocks.html: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. Copying errors in replication, radiation and some chemicals can cause them. What a mutation does depends on how it changes the codons you learned to read in Reading the Genetic Code.

A substitution swaps one base. It can be silent (same amino acid), missense (a different amino acid) or nonsense (a stop codon, so the protein is cut short). An insertion or deletion of one base shifts the reading frame: a frameshift changes every codon after it.

blocks.name: bi-central
blocks.cap: A missense mutation: UUU (Phe) became UUA (Leu).

blocks.html: The ribosome reads in threes from AUG with no commas. A substitution touches one codon only. An insertion or deletion moves every later base by one, so every later codon is read wrong, the way "THE CAT ATE THE RAT" becomes "THE CAA TET HER AT" if you drop one letter.

Effect
Type
rows: delete the A of UAC: AUG UCG GCU AA…
blocks.cap: One short gene, changed one base at a time (or with one base deleted).

blocks.title: Name the mutation
blocks.q: The mRNA AUG-CAU-GGA-UGA changes to AUG-CAC-GGA-UGA. What kind of mutation is it?
steps: Only the second codon changed: CAU → CAC.
CAU is His. CAC is also His.

blocks.title: A famous missense mutation
blocks.q: In sickle cell hemoglobin, one codon of the beta-globin gene changes from GAG to GUG. What changes in the protein?
steps: GAG codes for glutamic acid (Glu).
GUG codes for valine (Val).
blocks.a: One amino acid: Glu becomes Val. That single change alters how the hemoglobin behaves.

blocks.html: Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but a few help, and those are the raw material of natural selection. Only mutations in cells that become gametes are passed to offspring.

It is natural to think every substitution changes the protein. Many do not: most amino acids have several codons, so a change in the third base is often silent. In the other direction, one deleted base can garble the whole rest of a protein. Check by translating both versions, codon by codon.

blocks.html: A nerve cell and a skin cell in your body came from the same first cell by mitosis, so they carry the same DNA. Yet they look and work nothing alike. The difference is which genes each cell uses, which builds on translation.

Gene expression is using a gene to make its product. Cells switch genes on and off, mostly at transcription: proteins that bind DNA near a gene can block RNA polymerase or help it start. Different cell types express different genes from the same genome.

Making proteins costs energy and materials. A cell that made every protein all the time would waste both, and some proteins would get in each other's way. Regulation lets a cell make what it needs, when it needs it: a bacterium makes enzymes for a sugar only when that sugar is around, and a red blood cell precursor makes hemoglobin while a nerve cell does not.
In the 1960s François Jacob and Jacques Monod worked out how the bacterium E. coli controls its genes for digesting lactose, a milk sugar. The genes sit together under one switch, called an operon.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: No lactose: a repressor protein sits on the operator, so RNA polymerase is blocked
Lactose arrives: a form of it binds the repressor and changes its shape
The repressor lets go of the DNA
RNA polymerase transcribes the lactose genes
The enzymes digest the lactose; when it is gone, the repressor binds again
opts.title: The lac operon

blocks.cap: The lac genes turn on only when lactose is present.

blocks.title: Predicting the switch
blocks.q: A mutant E. coli makes a repressor that cannot bind the operator. Are the lactose genes on or off when there is no lactose?
steps: Normally the repressor blocks transcription when lactose is absent.
This repressor cannot sit on the DNA, so nothing blocks RNA polymerase.
blocks.a: On, all the time, even without lactose.

blocks.title: Another mutant
blocks.q: A different mutant repressor binds the operator but cannot bind lactose. What happens when lactose is present?
steps: Lactose normally pulls the repressor off the DNA.
This repressor ignores lactose and stays on.
blocks.a: The genes stay off, even with lactose.

blocks.html: Eukaryotes use many such DNA-binding proteins, called transcription factors, often in combinations. They also regulate at other steps: how DNA is packed, how RNA is processed, and how long a protein lasts. (The lac genes are also turned up most strongly when glucose, the bacterium's first choice, is scarce.)

People often think a nerve cell and a skin cell have different DNA. They have the same genes. They differ in which genes are expressed. Check with an example: a skin cell has the gene for the insulin protein too, but it keeps that gene switched off.

blocks.html: A drop of blood or a single hair holds only a tiny amount of DNA, far too little to study. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) makes billions of copies of one chosen piece. It is DNA replication done in a tube, over and over.

PCR repeats a cycle of three temperatures. Denature at about 95 °C: the strands separate. Anneal at about 50–65 °C: short primers bind on each side of the target. Extend at about 72 °C: a heat-proof DNA polymerase builds new strands. Each cycle doubles the target, so n cycles make $2^n$ copies of each starting copy.

Why doubling? Every copy made in one cycle becomes a template in the next. One copy becomes 2, then 4, then 8. That is exponential growth: after n cycles there are $2^n$ times as many copies. Thirty cycles give $2^{30}$, about a billion, in a couple of hours.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Copies of the target after each cycle: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64.

blocks.title: Counting copies
blocks.q: A tube starts with 5 copies of a gene. How many copies are there after 10 cycles?
steps: Each cycle doubles: 10 cycles multiply by $2^{10}$, which is 1,024.

blocks.title: How many cycles?
blocks.q: Starting from one copy, how many cycles are needed to pass one million copies?
steps: $2^{19}$ is 524,288, which is not enough.
$2^{20}$ is 1,048,576, which passes one million.

blocks.html: Two discoveries made PCR practical. Kary Mullis invented the method in 1983, and shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. And the DNA polymerase used comes from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from hot springs; this "Taq" polymerase survives the 95 °C step, so it does not have to be added again every cycle.

items: Primers are short single strands of DNA, about 20 bases, made to match the two ends of the target.
Only the stretch between the two primers is copied over and over.
Real reactions slow down after many cycles as primers and nucleotides run low, so $2^n$ is the ideal.

blocks.html: Two slips are common. One is adding instead of multiplying: 10 cycles do not make 10 or 20 copies, they make $2^{10}$ = 1,024 times as many. The other is thinking PCR copies a whole genome. It copies only the piece between the two primers. Check: the number of copies should double each time you add one cycle.

blocks.html: After PCR or after cutting DNA with enzymes, scientists need to see how big the pieces are. Gel electrophoresis sorts DNA pieces by length.

DNA is negatively charged, so in an electric field it moves toward the positive end. A gel is a mesh that slows big pieces more than small ones, so shorter pieces travel farther. A ladder of pieces with known sizes, run beside the samples, lets you read each band's size.

Every nucleotide has a phosphate group, and each phosphate carries a negative charge. So every DNA piece has about the same charge for each unit of length, and the electric pull per unit of length is the same for all of them. What sets them apart is the gel: a long piece has to snake through many more pores, so it falls behind.

blocks.name: bi-gel
blocks.cap: Samples load in wells at the negative end and run toward the positive end. Read sizes against the ladder.

blocks.title: Reading a gel
blocks.q: A sample has three bands: 3,000, 1,200 and 400 base pairs (bp). Which band ends up closest to the wells?
steps: Short pieces move farthest; long pieces stay near the wells.
The longest piece is 3,000 bp.

blocks.title: Cutting, then running
blocks.q: A straight (linear) DNA molecule of 5,000 bp is cut at two places, at 1,000 bp and at 3,500 bp from one end. What bands appear?
steps: The pieces run from 0 to 1,000, 1,000 to 3,500, and 3,500 to 5,000.
Their lengths: 1,000, 2,500 and 1,500 bp.
blocks.a: Three bands: 2,500, 1,500 and 1,000 bp (2,500 nearest the wells).

blocks.html: Gels are used to check that PCR worked, to compare DNA from different sources (a DNA profile compares band patterns at places where people differ in the number of repeats), and to pick out a gene for recombinant DNA. The DNA is invisible on its own, so it is stained with a dye that glows under special light.

Two ideas often get turned around. First, bigger pieces do not travel farther because they are heavier; they travel less far, because the gel holds them back. Second, DNA moves toward the positive electrode, because its phosphates are negative and opposite charges attract. Check: the smallest ladder band is always the one farthest from the wells.

blocks.html: People with diabetes once used insulin taken from the pancreas of cattle and pigs. Since the 1980s, human insulin has been made by microbes, such as bacteria, that carry the human insulin gene. That is recombinant DNA: DNA from two sources joined together. It uses gels and the idea of gene expression.

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific short sequences. DNA ligase joins pieces together. A gene can be cut out, joined into a plasmid (a small ring of bacterial DNA) and put into bacteria. The bacteria copy the plasmid as they divide and express the gene, making its protein.

It works because the genetic code is shared by nearly all life. A bacterium reads the codons of a human gene the same way a human cell does, so it builds the same chain of amino acids. A restriction enzyme cuts both the gene's DNA and the plasmid at the same sequence, leaving matching "sticky ends" that pair up so ligase can seal them.

blocks.name: bi-feedback

steps: Cut the human DNA and the plasmid with the same restriction enzyme
Mix them: the sticky ends of the gene and the opened plasmid pair up
DNA ligase seals the joins, making a recombinant plasmid
Bacteria take up the plasmid
The bacteria multiply and express the gene, making the human protein

blocks.cap: The steps in order.

blocks.title: A restriction site
blocks.q: The enzyme EcoRI cuts at the sequence GAATTC. How many times does it cut the strand GGAATTCATTGAATTCAA?
steps: Search for GAATTC: it starts at the 2nd base.
Search again after it: it starts at the 11th base.
No others.

blocks.title: Counting pieces
blocks.q: A plasmid is a closed ring. If an enzyme cuts it at 3 places, how many pieces form? What if the DNA were a straight line cut at 3 places?
steps: A ring cut once opens into one piece; each later cut adds a piece. So 3 cuts make 3 pieces.
A line cut once makes 2 pieces; 3 cuts make 4.

blocks.html: EcoRI reads GAATTC on both strands (the sequence is the same read 5′→3′ on either strand) and cuts each strand between the G and the first A, leaving four unpaired bases, AATT, on each end. Human insulin made by bacteria was approved for use in the United States in 1982, the first medicine made with recombinant DNA. Crops can be engineered in similar ways; people weigh the benefits and concerns of those crops differently, while the laboratory methods themselves are well established.

It is easy to assume bacteria cannot read a human gene, since bacteria and people are so different. But the genetic code is nearly universal: the same codons mean the same amino acids in both. (Human genes do contain introns, which bacteria cannot remove, so scientists insert a version of the gene with the introns already taken out.)

blocks.html: In middle school you saw how natural selection works in a story. In 1858 Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace each proposed it, and Darwin laid out the evidence in On the Origin of Species in 1859. Here we state it as four facts and the conclusion that follows from them.

items: Variation: individuals in a population differ in their traits.
Heritability: many of those differences are passed from parents to offspring, because they come from alleles (see How Meiosis Makes Variation).
More offspring than can survive: populations produce more young than the food, space and shelter can support.
Differences in survival and reproduction: individuals whose traits suit the environment tend to leave more offspring.

blocks.html: If all four are true, the helpful heritable traits become more common in the population generation after generation. That change is evolution by natural selection. Individuals do not evolve; populations do.

Nothing here needs a plan or a goal. It is bookkeeping. If dark beetles on dark soil are eaten less often, more of the next generation has parents with alleles for dark color, so the share of those alleles goes up. Repeat over many generations and the population changes.

blocks.name: bi-selection
blocks.cap: Birds catch the beetles they can see. Press Next generation a few times and watch the average color.

blocks.title: Following the numbers
blocks.q: A population of 100 beetles is 50 light and 50 dark, on dark soil. Birds eat 60% of the light beetles and 20% of the dark ones. What share of the survivors are dark?
steps: Light survivors: 40% of 50 = 20.
Dark survivors: 80% of 50 = 40.

blocks.html: Biologists measure success by fitness: how many offspring an individual leaves that survive to have offspring of their own. A trait is "fit" only in a particular place. Dark beetles are fit on dark soil and easy prey on light sand.

"Survival of the fittest" makes people think of the strongest or fastest animal. In biology, fitness means leaving more offspring in a particular environment. A small, plain, slow moth that hides well and lays many eggs can be fitter than a big strong one. And a trait that helps in one place can hurt in another.

blocks.html: For a polygenic trait like body size, a population forms a bell-shaped curve. Natural selection can push on that curve in three ways, and each leaves its own mark on the graph.

Directional selection favors one extreme, so the whole curve shifts that way. Stabilizing selection favors the middle, so the curve gets narrower and taller. Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle, so the curve spreads and can split into two peaks.

blocks.name: bi-chart

opts.title: The same population under two kinds of selection

blocks.cap: Stabilizing selection narrows the curve around the middle; disruptive selection lowers the middle and raises both ends.

blocks.html: Ask which individuals leave the most offspring. If the largest do best, the next generation's average moves up: directional. If the middle does best and both extremes do poorly, the spread shrinks: stabilizing. If both extremes do well and the middle does poorly, the middle thins out: disruptive.

Who does best
Curve after
Example

blocks.title: Reading a graph
blocks.q: Before selection, a lizard population's body lengths center on 10 cm with a wide spread. Later the center is still 10 cm, but the spread is much narrower. Which pattern?
steps: The average did not move, so not directional.
The curve did not split.
The extremes became rarer.

blocks.title: Another graph
blocks.q: A trait's average moves from 4 mm to 6 mm over many generations, with the same spread. Which pattern?
steps: The whole curve moved toward larger values.

blocks.html: Stabilizing and disruptive are easy to mix up because both keep the average in about the same place. Look at the middle of the curve. Stabilizing makes the middle taller and the sides thinner; disruptive makes the middle lower and the sides taller.

blocks.html: Evolution usually takes many generations, but when selection is strong and generations are short, we can watch it. These cases put directional selection and populations changing over time on a timeline you can see.

When an antibiotic is used, it kills the bacteria it can. A few bacteria may already carry an allele that lets them survive. Those survivors multiply, so the next population is mostly resistant. The CDC describes resistance as germs developing "the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them," and notes that antibiotics do not work on viruses. Insects become resistant to pesticides the same way.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: After the drug, a single resistant survivor that doubles each generation becomes 64 resistant bacteria in six generations.

blocks.html: On the small Galápagos island of Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured medium ground finches year after year. In the 1977 drought, small soft seeds ran out and the population fell by about 85%. Birds with deeper beaks could crack the hard seeds that were left, so more of them survived. Their offspring also had deeper beaks on average: evolution measured in one generation.

In each case the variation was already there. The drug, the pesticide or the drought did not create the helpful trait. It selected among traits that already varied, and the next generation inherited the survivors' alleles.

A mutation is a copying change, and copying changes happen whether or not they would help. The environment cannot reach into the DNA and order the right one. What the environment does is decide who leaves offspring. That is why resistance spreads faster when a drug is used more: more use means stronger selection.

blocks.title: Counting survivors
blocks.q: A colony of 1,000,000 bacteria has 10 resistant cells. An antibiotic kills every other cell. The survivors double every hour. How many bacteria are there 5 hours later?
steps: Survivors: the 10 resistant cells.
Five doublings multiply by $2^5 = 32$.

blocks.html: A very common idea is that the drug or the drought caused the needed change, as if the bacteria "learned" to resist. The variation was there first; the environment only chose among it. A quick check: in the finch study, the deep beaks were measured before the drought began.

blocks.html: If living species share ancestors, the past should leave traces: fossils of in-between forms, and bodies built from the same parts. In Comparing Body Structures you met the idea. Here is the evidence in more detail; natural selection explains how the changes happened.

Transitional fossils show mixes of old and new features. Homologous structures are the same parts, inherited from a common ancestor, used for different jobs. Vestigial structures are reduced parts with little or no use left. All three point to common ancestry.

items: Tiktaalik, found in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada, lived about 375 million years ago. It was a fish with gills and scales, but with a flat head, a neck and sturdy fins with wrist-like bones: a step toward four-legged animals.

Early whales: Pakicetus, about 50 million years old, was a land mammal with an ear like a whale's. Later fossils show legs shrinking as whale ancestors moved into the sea. DNA links whales to hippos and other hoofed mammals.
The forelimb: a human arm, a whale flipper, a bat wing and a cat leg have the same bones in the same order, built for different jobs.
Vestigial parts: whales still have small hip bones; some snakes have tiny leg spurs; cave fish have eyes that do not see.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: Each new trait appears once on the tree, and every group branching after it inherits it. Four limbs appear on the branch leading to frogs, lizards and mice.

blocks.html: Why would a whale have hip bones, or a bat wing have the same bones as your arm? Engineers designing each animal fresh would not need to reuse parts. But evolution can only modify what an ancestor already had, so old parts get reshaped, and parts that lose their job shrink but linger.

blocks.title: Homologous or analogous?
blocks.q: Are a bird's wing and a butterfly's wing homologous?
steps: Both are used for flying.
But a bird wing has the bones of a vertebrate forelimb; an insect wing is a thin outgrowth of the exoskeleton with no bones.
They evolved separately for the same job.
blocks.a: No. They are analogous, not homologous.

blocks.html: Analogous structures, like the wings of birds and insects, or the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins, look alike because they do the same job. They are not evidence of close kinship. Only homologous structures, the same parts doing different jobs, show shared ancestry. Check: look at the inner structure, not the outer use.

blocks.html: Fossils and bones are one record of ancestry; DNA is another. Every species carries a copy of its ancestors' genes, changed a little by mutations along the way. Comparing sequences, which you can read with the genetic code, confirms the story told by fossils and anatomy.

Two species that shared a common ancestor more recently have had less time to collect differences, so their DNA and protein sequences are more alike. Counting the differences in the same gene or protein lets us compare how closely species are related.

After two populations split, each collects its own mutations, generation after generation. Like two copies of a book recopied by hand in two places, the longer they have been apart, the more differences pile up. So the number of differences works like a rough clock since the split.

blocks.title: Counting differences
blocks.q:
Part of a protein in four species:
Species W: Met-Gly-Lys-Val-Ala-His
Species X: Met-Gly-Lys-Ile-Ala-His
Species Y: Met-Ala-Arg-Ile-Ala-His
Which species is most closely related to W?
steps: W vs X: one difference (Val/Ile).
W vs Y: three differences (Gly/Ala, Lys/Arg, Val/Ile).
blocks.a: Species X, with the fewest differences.

blocks.cap: Tap two primates to light up their most recent common ancestor. Humans and chimpanzees share one; neither descends from the other.

blocks.html: Humans and chimpanzees are a good example. In the parts of their genomes that line up, about 98.8% of the DNA bases are the same. That is why they sit next to each other on the tree. Gorillas are a bit less similar, orangutans less again, matching the order of branching that fossils and anatomy suggest.

blocks.title: Reading the clock
blocks.q: A gene differs at 6 bases between species A and B, at 6 between A and C, and at 2 between B and C. Which two shared the most recent common ancestor?
steps: The smallest difference is between B and C.
A differs from both by the same amount, so A branched off first.

blocks.html: Because human and chimpanzee DNA is so similar, people sometimes say humans evolved from chimpanzees. They did not. Both species descend from a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago, and each line has changed since. Living chimpanzees are our cousins, not our ancestors.

blocks.html: A phylogenetic tree is a diagram of ancestry. It turns the evidence from DNA and proteins and from fossils into a picture you can read. Reading it correctly takes one rule.

Each branch point (node) stands for a common ancestor. Two species are more closely related when their most recent common ancestor is more recent, that is, when you reach a shared node sooner by tracing back from the tips. Distance across the tips on the page means nothing.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: Tap two tips to find their most recent common ancestor. A frog's closest relative here is the lizard-and-mouse group, not the perch.

blocks.html: A tree records splits. Tracing back from two tips, the first node where their lines meet is the last population they both came from. Everything after that node happened separately. The more recent that node, the less separate history the two species have.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: Tap a node to rotate its branches. The order of the tips changes, but no relationship changes: like a mobile, the branches can spin.

blocks.title: Who is closer?
blocks.q: On the vertebrate tree, is a perch more closely related to a shark or to a mouse?
steps: Trace the perch and the mouse back: they meet at the node of all bony vertebrates.
Trace the perch and the shark back: they meet farther back, at the node of all jawed vertebrates.
The perch-mouse ancestor is more recent.
blocks.a: To the mouse. (A perch and a mouse share a more recent ancestor than a perch and a shark.)

blocks.title: Reading a clade
blocks.q: On the same tree, which organisms descend from the ancestor where four limbs first appeared?
steps: Find the trait mark for four limbs.
Every tip to the right of that mark descends from it.

blocks.html: A clade is an ancestor and all of its descendants: cut one branch of the tree and everything on it is a clade. Fish, as the word is used every day, is not a clade, because the ancestor of all fish is also the ancestor of frogs, lizards and mice.

Two misreadings are common. One is judging kinship by which tips sit next to each other on the page; rotating a node moves the tips without changing the tree. The other is calling the species at the right end "more evolved". Every living tip has been evolving for exactly the same length of time since the root; only the branch points show kinship.

blocks.html: A cladogram is a phylogenetic tree built from shared traits. To build one you need to tell new traits from old ones.

Group organisms by shared derived traits: new features that some of the organisms have and others lack. The trait that all but one organism share marks the first branch (that one is the outgroup). Each trait shared by fewer organisms marks a smaller group nested inside.

A derived trait appeared once, in one ancestor, and was passed to all its descendants. So everyone with that trait belongs to one branch. A trait that all the organisms have, like a backbone in a set of vertebrates, came from before the whole group and cannot sort them.

blocks.html: Two mistakes: grouping by overall look ("a shark looks like a perch, so they go together") and grouping by traits everyone shares. Looks can come from similar ways of life. Shared old traits tell you nothing about the branches. Only derived traits, present in some and missing in others, mark branches.

blocks.html: To see whether a population is evolving, we need to know what "not evolving" looks like. In 1908 the mathematician G. H. Hardy and the physician Wilhelm Weinberg each worked it out, using the product rule and square roots.

For a gene with alleles A and a, let p be the frequency of A and q the frequency of a, so $p + q = 1$. In a population that is not evolving, the genotype frequencies are $$p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$$ (AA, Aa, aa), and p and q stay the same each generation.

Imagine all the gametes of the population in one pool. A gamete carries A with chance p and a with chance q. If parents pair up at random, an offspring gets two gametes independently: AA with chance $p \times p = p^2$, aa with chance $q^2$, and Aa two ways (A then a, or a then A), $2pq$. It is a Punnett square for a whole population.

blocks.name: bi-punnett
blocks.cap: With p = q = ½ the square gives ¼ AA, ½ Aa, ¼ aa. In general the boxes are p², pq, pq and q².

blocks.title: Starting from the recessive share
blocks.q: In a population, 16% of individuals show a recessive trait. Find q, p and the share of carriers.
steps: Recessive individuals are aa, so $q^2 = 0.16$.
Carriers: $2pq = 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.48$.

blocks.title: From counts
blocks.q: A sample has 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals. What is p?
steps: There are 100 individuals, so 200 alleles.

items: The equilibrium holds only when no evolution is going on: no mutation, no migration (gene flow), a very large population (no drift), parents pair up at random, and no natural selection.
Real populations rarely meet all five, so Hardy-Weinberg is a baseline: if measured frequencies differ from it, something is changing the population (see the mechanisms of evolution).

blocks.html: Two classic slips. One is taking q to be the share of recessive-looking individuals. That share is $q^2$; take its square root to get q. The other is thinking dominant alleles must become more common over time. Dominance only decides which allele shows. Without selection or another force, p and q do not change at all.

blocks.html: Hardy-Weinberg tells us what happens when nothing changes allele frequencies. Four forces do change them. Natural selection is only one.

Allele frequencies change by mutation (new alleles), genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), gene flow (alleles carried in or out by migrating individuals or pollen) and natural selection (alleles that help survival and reproduction become more common).

Drift is the law of small numbers. Flip a coin 10 times and you may get 7 heads; flip it 10,000 times and you will be very close to half. In a small population, which individuals happen to leave offspring is partly luck, so allele frequencies wander. In a large one, the luck averages out.

items: Bottleneck: a disaster leaves a few survivors, whose alleles are a random sample. Hunting cut northern elephant seals to perhaps 20 to 100 animals by the 1890s. Under protection they now number well over 100,000, but they have very little genetic variation.
Founder effect: a few individuals start a new population, such as on an island, carrying only some of the old population's alleles.
Gene flow makes neighboring populations more alike; cutting it off lets them drift and adapt apart.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: An example of drift: by chance, the small population lost allele a entirely, while the large one barely moved.

blocks.title: A founder population
blocks.q: Ten birds blown to an island start a new population. Among their 20 alleles for a gene, 6 are a. What is q in the new population, if the mainland has q = 0.1?
steps: q = 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3 on the island.
The founders were a small, chance sample of the mainland birds.
blocks.a: q = 0.3, three times the mainland value, by chance alone.

blocks.title: Naming the force
blocks.q: Pollen from a field of one kind of corn blows into a neighboring field, bringing alleles the second field lacked. Which mechanism is this?
steps: Alleles are moving between populations.

blocks.html: It is natural to think every evolutionary change is an adaptation. Drift changes frequencies by chance, with no regard to whether an allele helps. In a small population, drift can even make a harmful allele common, or fix it so every individual has it. Ask: is this change better explained by advantage, or by small numbers and luck?

blocks.html: A species, for most plants and animals, is a group of populations that can exchange genes with one another, producing offspring that can themselves have offspring. A new species forms when one population splits into two that stop exchanging genes. The mechanisms of evolution then change each part on its own.

Speciation starts when gene flow stops. Often a barrier divides a population (geographic isolation): a river, a mountain range, a new sea. Without a barrier, populations can split by using different habitats or by timing, such as flowering in different seasons. In plants, a doubled chromosome set (polyploidy) can make a new species in one generation.

Once two populations no longer exchange alleles, each one's mutations, drift and selection stay with it. Over many generations the differences pile up until, even if the two meet again, their gametes no longer combine well or their hybrids cannot survive or cannot themselves have offspring. Then they are separate species.

blocks.name: bi-tree
blocks.cap: One ancestral population, split by a barrier, becomes two branches on the tree.

items: Geographic: when the Isthmus of Panama rose, it split sea animals into Caribbean and Pacific populations, which have since become different species.
Habitat: two groups of the same insect may come to live on different host plants in the same area.
Timing: two plant populations that flower in different months cannot pollinate each other.
Polyploidy: bread wheat has six sets of chromosomes (2n = 42), the result of hybrids between three ancestral species whose chromosome sets doubled.

blocks.title: Polyploidy in numbers
blocks.q: A plant species has 2n = 14. A cell division error doubles every chromosome, making a plant with 28. Can it make normal offspring with the original species?
steps: The new plant makes gametes with 14 chromosomes; the original makes gametes with 7.
A combination of 14 and 7 gives 21, an odd number with no partner for many chromosomes, so such offspring usually cannot themselves have offspring.
blocks.a: No: the 28-chromosome plants are a new species, isolated in one step.

blocks.html: Two misconceptions are common. One is that a new species appears suddenly from one big mutation in an animal. Most speciation is gradual, through many small changes. The other is that speciation always needs a physical barrier; habitat, timing and, in plants, polyploidy can split populations living side by side.

blocks.html: In Limiting Factors and Carrying Capacity you saw that populations cannot grow forever. Two simple models describe how they grow, and they use the exponential growth you know from algebra.

With unlimited resources, a population grows exponentially: $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN$, a J-shaped curve. As resources run short, growth slows and the population levels off at the carrying capacity K: logistic growth, $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\frac{K - N}{K}$, an S-shaped curve.

In exponential growth, every individual adds offspring at the same rate r, so more individuals means faster growth: the rate is proportional to N. In logistic growth the extra factor $\frac{K - N}{K}$ is the share of the habitat still unused. When N is small it is nearly 1, so growth looks exponential; when N reaches K it is 0, so growth stops.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: The J-curve and the S-curve start alike. Drag the sliders to change r and K.

blocks.title: Exponential growth rate
blocks.q: A population of 400 rabbits has r = 0.3 per year with plenty of food. How fast is it growing?
steps: $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN = 0.3 \times 400$.

blocks.title: Logistic growth rate
blocks.q: The same population lives where K = 1,000. How fast does it grow at N = 400? At N = 900?
steps: At 900: $0.3 \times 900 \times \frac{100}{1000} = 27$ per year.
blocks.a: 72 per year at N = 400, and only 27 per year at N = 900.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Logistic growth is fastest at N = K/2, where the curve is steepest.

blocks.html: Why is K/2 the fastest point? Growth is r × N × (share of room left). At N = K/2 there are many individuals and half the room is still free. Below that there are too few individuals; above it there is too little room. The product is largest exactly in the middle.

It is tempting to think growth is fastest when the population is biggest, near K. In logistic growth it is fastest at about half of K, then slows as the population fills its habitat. Check with numbers: at N = K the growth rate is $rK \times 0 = 0$.
Real populations only roughly follow these models, and many overshoot K and dip back. See how predators and prey push each other up and down in the Predators and Prey simulation.

blocks.html: Every population in the logistic model is held near its carrying capacity by something. Ecologists sort those limits into two kinds, by one question: does crowding make it worse?

Density-dependent factors hit harder as a population gets more crowded: competition for food, disease, predation, waste and stress. Density-independent factors hit no matter how crowded: floods, fires, hard frosts, droughts, hurricanes.

In a crowded population, each animal has less food, meets sick neighbors more often, and is easier for predators to find. So the death rate per individual rises with density, which pulls the population back down: that is negative feedback, and it is what produces a carrying capacity. A hurricane, by contrast, kills about the same share of the trees whether the forest is thick or thin.

cards.text: A disease that spreads by contact
More predators drawn to a crowded herd
cards.why: Predators find and catch more prey where prey are dense.

blocks.title: Reading data
blocks.q: In years when a deer herd had 200 deer, 5% died over winter. In years with 600 deer, 20% died. Is the main cause of death density dependent?
steps: The death rate (the percent) rose as the herd grew.
That is the mark of a density-dependent factor, such as food running short.

blocks.title: A second case
blocks.q: A frost kills about 30% of an insect population every time, whether the insects are few or many. Which kind of factor is the frost?
steps: The percent killed does not change with density.

blocks.html: Density-dependent factors work like a thermostat on population size: they push harder the farther the population rises. Density-independent factors are more like random shocks that knock a population down whatever its size. Real populations feel both, often in the same year.

People often call every limiting factor density dependent, because any limit "limits" the population. Ask a sharper question: does the effect on each individual grow with crowding? A hurricane does not care how dense the population is; a contagious disease does.

blocks.html: A community is all the populations living in one place. In middle school you named the interactions between them. Here we add the idea of a niche, and what happens when two species need the same one.

A species' niche is its role and needs: what it eats, when it is active, where it shelters, what conditions it tolerates. Its habitat is only where it lives. Two species cannot share exactly the same niche for long: one outcompetes the other (competitive exclusion).

If two species need exactly the same limited resource in the same way, any small advantage lets one take a bit more each generation, and the other shrinks. In the 1930s Georgii Gause grew two kinds of Paramecium on the same food. Alone, each grew well. Together, one always drove the other out. Species that do coexist usually split the resource: they eat at different times, in different spots or different sizes of food (resource partitioning).

blocks.title: Coexisting competitors
blocks.q: Two warbler species feed on insects in the same spruce trees. One feeds near the treetops, the other on the lower branches. Why can both survive there?
steps: They live in the same habitat.
But they feed in different parts of the trees, so they do not compete fully.
blocks.a: They partition the resource, so their niches differ.

blocks.html: Habitat and niche are easy to confuse. The habitat is the address: where the species lives. The niche is the job: how it lives there, what it eats, when it is active and what it needs. Many species share one habitat, but each has its own niche.

blocks.html: You met energy pyramids in Energy Pyramids. Now that you know cellular respiration, you can see where the "lost" energy goes.

Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight captured by producers, and flows up through trophic levels: primary consumers, secondary consumers and so on. On average only about 10% of the energy at one level becomes the bodies of the next. The rest is used for living and released as heat.

An animal eats food, but it does not turn all of it into new body. Some is not digested and leaves as waste. Most of what is absorbed is burned in cellular respiration to power moving, breathing and keeping warm, and that energy ends up as heat. Only what is stored in new tissue is available to the next eater. Energy is never destroyed (that is the law of conservation of energy); it just leaves the food chain as heat that no organism can use.

blocks.name: bi-pyramid
blocks.cap: Each level holds about a tenth of the energy of the level below it. Drag the slider to try other transfer shares.

blocks.title: Up the pyramid
blocks.q: Producers in a meadow capture 50,000 kcal per square meter in a year. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
steps: Primary consumers: 10% of 50,000 = 5,000 kcal.
Secondary consumers: 10% of 5,000 = 500 kcal.
blocks.a: About 500 kcal per square meter per year.

blocks.title: Measuring efficiency
blocks.q: Herbivores in a pond store 1,200 kcal; the fish that eat them store 90 kcal. What is the transfer efficiency?
steps: Efficiency = energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the lower level.

blocks.html: Because so much energy is lost at each step, food chains rarely have more than four or five levels, and top predators are few. Biomass (the mass of living things) and numbers usually shrink up the pyramid too, though not always: one large tree can feed thousands of insects, so a pyramid of numbers can be upside down.

Two errors are common. One is treating the 10% rule as exact; it is a rough average, and real transfers range from about 5% to 20%. The other is thinking the lost energy is destroyed. It is not: it is used in respiration and given off as heat, which flows out of the ecosystem.

blocks.html: Energy flows through an ecosystem and out as heat, but matter is recycled. The atoms in your body have been in rocks, air and other living things. Photosynthesis, Respiration and the Carbon Cycle and The Nitrogen Cycle started the story; here are three cycles side by side.

Carbon moves from the air into living things by photosynthesis and back by respiration, decomposition and burning; the ocean and fossil fuels are large stores. Nitrogen is cycled mostly by bacteria: fixation (N₂ → ammonia), nitrification (ammonia → nitrate), and denitrification (nitrate → N₂). Phosphorus cycles slowly through rock, soil, water and living things, with no gas phase.

blocks.name: bi-cycle
blocks.cap: The carbon cycle. Tap a process to see where carbon goes.

blocks.html: Why do living things need these elements? Carbon is the backbone of every biological molecule. Nitrogen is in every amino acid and every base of DNA. Phosphorus is in DNA's backbone, in ATP and in membranes. Since the planet gets almost no new atoms, life must reuse the ones it has.

blocks.name: bi-cycle
blocks.cap: The nitrogen cycle. Air is about 78% nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use N₂ until bacteria (or lightning) fix it.

blocks.title: Following a nitrogen atom
blocks.q: Trace a nitrogen atom from the air into a rabbit.
steps: Bacteria in the soil, or in the root nodules of plants such as beans, fix N₂ into ammonia.
Other bacteria turn ammonia into nitrate.
A plant's roots take up the nitrate and use it to build amino acids.
A rabbit eats the plant.
blocks.a: Air → fixation → nitrification → roots → plant protein → rabbit.

blocks.name: bi-cycle
blocks.cap: The phosphorus cycle: weathering releases phosphate from rock; it passes through soil, water and living things, and settles back into sediment.

blocks.html: People speed up some steps. Burning fossil fuels moves carbon from long-term stores into the air faster than photosynthesis takes it back. Nitrogen and phosphorus spread on farm fields can wash into lakes and feed blooms of algae. How best to manage these changes is debated, and the trade-offs involve farming, energy and cost; the cycles themselves are well understood.

It is natural to think every element cycles through the air the way carbon and nitrogen do. Phosphorus does not: it has no significant gas form. It moves through rocks, soil, water and organisms, and its slowest step, rock forming and then weathering, takes millions of years.

blocks.html: Most of the life you can see uses oxygen. But in waterlogged soil, the mud at the bottom of a pond, or deep in a compost pile, oxygen runs out. Life goes on there, using fermentation and other pathways, and that changes how matter cycles.

Aerobic means with oxygen; anaerobic means without. In anaerobic places many microbes still release energy from food by fermentation or by passing electrons to something other than oxygen, such as nitrate. Some microbes cannot survive oxygen at all.

Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration, and it makes the most ATP. Without it, cells must use other acceptors, which give less energy, or ferment, which gives only 2 ATP per glucose. Water fills the spaces between soil grains and oxygen diffuses through water about 10,000 times more slowly than through air, so a flooded soil quickly runs out of it.

blocks.name: bi-energy
blocks.cap: Aerobic respiration: glycolysis, then the stages in the mitochondrion that need oxygen. Without oxygen, only glycolysis runs, kept going by fermentation.

items: Denitrification: in waterlogged soil, bacteria use nitrate instead of oxygen and release nitrogen gas, so wet soils lose nitrogen to the air.
Methane: archaea in wetlands, rice paddies and the stomachs of cattle make methane (CH₄) as they break down matter without oxygen.
Slow decay: without oxygen, dead plants break down slowly, so peat builds up in bogs. Over very long times, buried dead matter became coal and other fossil fuels.

blocks.q: A soil is flooded for weeks. What happens to its nitrate, and why?
steps: Water fills the air spaces, so oxygen runs out.
Denitrifying bacteria then use nitrate in place of oxygen.
They turn it into nitrogen gas, which escapes to the air.
blocks.a: The nitrate falls as it is turned into N₂ gas.

blocks.title: Comparing energy
blocks.q: Per glucose, fermentation makes 2 ATP and aerobic respiration about 30. About how many times more ATP does aerobic respiration make?

blocks.html: People often think life stops without oxygen. Many microbes thrive without it, and some cannot live with it at all. Your own muscle cells can run briefly without oxygen by fermentation. Check the place: waterlogged soil, mud and the gut are full of anaerobic life.

blocks.html: A healthy ecosystem is not frozen. Succession showed that communities change over years. And community interactions keep populations rising and falling. So what does "stable" mean?

An ecosystem is stable when its populations and processes stay within a range over time, even as they go up and down. Small disturbances, like a storm, are followed by recovery. A large or lasting change, like a new predator, the loss of a key species or a changed climate, can shift the ecosystem to a new state.

Negative feedback holds populations in a range: more prey feed more predators, who then eat the prey down, so both swing but stay bounded. A disturbance pushes populations off course, and the same feedbacks pull them back, as long as the push is small and the key species survive. Push hard enough, or remove a species that the feedbacks depend on, and different feedbacks take over.

blocks.name: bi-population
blocks.cap: Predators and prey rise and fall in turns, but stay within a range: a stable, not a fixed, system.

blocks.title: Reading a record
blocks.q: A pond's fish population was counted every year: 410, 450, 380, 430, 150 (after a drought), 300, 420, 440. Is the pond stable?
steps: In normal years the count stays between about 380 and 450.
The drought pushed it down, and within two years it was back in the range.
blocks.a: Yes: it fluctuates within a range and recovered from the disturbance.

blocks.title: A shift
blocks.q: In some kelp forests, after sea otters were hunted out, sea urchins multiplied and ate the kelp down to bare rock. The barren state lasted for years. Was this a recovery or a shift?
steps: The ecosystem did not return to its old range.
A different set of populations took over and held steady.
blocks.a: A shift to a new state.

blocks.html: Ecosystems with more species, and with several species doing the same job, often recover better, because if one species is lost, another can fill in. This is one reason scientists study biodiversity.

A balanced ecosystem is sometimes imagined as one where nothing changes. Populations always fluctuate. Stability means they stay within a range and come back after small upsets, not that they hold one fixed value.
