blocks.html: Some species matter far more than their numbers suggest. You saw in Stability, Disturbance and Change that losing one species can shift a whole ecosystem, and in Energy Flow that predators are few. Put those together and you get the keystone species.

A keystone species has a much larger effect on its ecosystem than its numbers or mass would suggest. Removing it sets off a trophic cascade: effects that pass down the food chain, level by level, each level rising or falling in turn.

A cascade alternates. If a top predator is removed, its prey increases; with more prey eating them, the level below that decreases; and the level below that increases. Each step flips the sign. So removing one predator can end up wiping out the plants two levels down.

items: The ochre sea star: in the 1960s ecologist Robert Paine removed the sea star Pisaster from patches of rocky shore in Washington. Mussels it had been eating took over the rock and crowded out many other species. In 1969 he coined the term "keystone species" for it.
Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze kelp. Where otters disappeared, urchins boomed and stripped the kelp forests; where otters returned, kelp came back.

Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995. Elk changed in number and behavior. How much of the later change in streamside plants comes from the wolves, and how much from other causes, is still studied and debated by ecologists.

blocks.title: Following a cascade
blocks.q: In a lake, bass eat minnows, minnows eat water fleas, and water fleas eat algae. Fishing removes most of the bass. What happens to the algae?

More minnows: water fleas decrease.
Fewer water fleas: algae increase.

More deer: more young trees eaten.

blocks.html: It is natural to think the most numerous species must be the most important. Keystone species are often uncommon predators. The sea star was far less common than the mussels it ate, yet the whole shore community depended on it. Importance is measured by effect, not by count.

blocks.html: Many animals live in groups: herds of zebras, flocks of starlings, schools of sardines, packs of wolves. In Community Interactions you looked at how species affect each other. Here the question is why individuals of one species stay together, and the answer comes from natural selection.

Group behavior persists because it helps the individuals who do it survive and leave offspring. Common benefits: many eyes spot predators sooner; the dilution effect spreads the risk (a predator that takes one animal from a group of 50 takes you with chance 1 in 50); predators can be confused by a swirling school; and group members can hunt together for prey too big to catch alone.

Natural selection acts on the alleles that individuals pass on. An animal that stays in the middle of the herd is less likely to be eaten than one alone at the edge, so behaviors that keep an animal in a group are favored even though no animal is "trying" to help the herd. Groups have costs too: more competition for food and faster spread of disease.

blocks.cap: The dilution effect: if a predator takes one animal per attack, each animal's chance is 1 divided by the group size.

blocks.title: The dilution effect
blocks.q: A hawk catches one pigeon per attack. What is a pigeon's chance of being the one caught if it is alone? In a flock of 25?
steps: Alone: 1 in 1, or 100%.
In a flock of 25: 1 in 25 = 4%.

blocks.title: Many eyes
blocks.q: Ostriches in larger groups each spend less time looking up for predators, and more time feeding, yet the group spots predators at least as fast. Why?
steps: With more birds, someone is almost always looking.
So each bird can look up less often without the group being caught off guard.
blocks.a: Shared vigilance: more eyes let each individual feed more.

blocks.html: A common idea is that animals form groups for the good of the group or the species. Group behavior is kept by selection because it raises the survival of the individuals who do it. A pigeon in a flock is safer itself; that is enough for flocking to spread.

blocks.html: Biodiversity is the variety of life: of genes, of species and of ecosystems. It connects to keystone species and to how ecosystems recover from disturbances. To compare places, ecologists need to measure it.

Species diversity has two parts. Richness is how many species there are. Evenness is how equal their numbers are. Simpson's diversity index combines both: $$D = 1 - \sum p_i^2$$ where $p_i$ is the share of individuals belonging to species i. D runs from 0 (one species) toward 1 (many species in even numbers).

$\sum p_i^2$ is the chance that two individuals picked at random belong to the same species. If one species makes up nearly everything, that chance is high and D is low. If many species share the community evenly, two random picks rarely match, so D is high.

blocks.title: Two forests
blocks.q: Forest 1 has 4 tree species, 25 trees each. Forest 2 has the same 4 species: 85, 5, 5 and 5 trees. Compare their Simpson indexes.
blocks.a: Same richness, but Forest 1 is far more diverse (D = 0.75 against 0.27).

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: Same four species, very different evenness.

blocks.html: The main threats to biodiversity are well established: habitat loss (the largest), invasive species, pollution, overharvesting and climate change. Solutions involve trade-offs that communities weigh differently, such as protecting land versus using it for farms, homes or jobs, and the costs of controlling invasive species. Scientists contribute evidence on what each option is likely to do; choosing among them is a decision for the people affected.

It is natural to count only the number of species. Two forests with ten species each are not equally diverse if one is 91% a single species. Check evenness too: a high Simpson index needs both many species and fairly equal numbers.
You can record what lives near you, a good first step in measuring biodiversity, with Nature Study.

blocks.html: Your enzymes work best in a narrow range of temperature and pH (see Temperature, pH and Enzymes). So your body works hard to keep its inside steady, whatever happens outside. That steadiness is homeostasis.

Homeostasis keeps conditions inside the body within a narrow range around a set point. Most of it runs on negative feedback: a sensor detects a change, a control center compares it with the set point, and effectors act to reverse the change. Positive feedback does the opposite: it amplifies a change until some event ends it.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: A negative feedback loop. Switch between too hot and too cold: the response always pushes back toward the set point.

blocks.html: A home thermostat is the classic model. When the room cools below the setting, the sensor tells the control box, which switches the furnace on; the room warms, and the furnace switches off. The response undoes the change that triggered it, which is why it is called negative. Because the fix starts only after a change is sensed, the value wobbles a little around the set point rather than holding perfectly still.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Positive feedback: platelets at a cut release chemicals that call more platelets, which release more chemicals, until a clot seals the wound.

blocks.title: Negative or positive?
blocks.q: As a fruit ripens it gives off ethylene gas, which makes nearby fruit ripen and give off more ethylene. Which kind of feedback is this?
steps: The response (more ethylene) makes the change (ripening) bigger, not smaller.
It stops only when the fruit are ripe.

blocks.title: Naming the parts
blocks.q: Blood sugar rises after a meal. Cells in the pancreas detect it and release insulin, and body cells take up glucose. Which is the sensor, and which the effector?
steps: The pancreas cells detect the change: sensor (and here also the control center).
Body cells and the liver, acting on insulin, carry out the response: effectors.
blocks.a: Sensor: pancreas cells. Effectors: body cells and the liver.

blocks.html: Two misreadings. "Negative" does not mean bad, and "positive" does not mean good: negative feedback reverses a change, positive feedback amplifies one. And homeostasis does not hold values perfectly fixed; they wobble within a range around the set point.

blocks.html: Your body's core stays near 37 °C, on a cold winter morning or a hot summer afternoon. It is the clearest example of the negative feedback you just learned.

The hypothalamus in the brain is the control center. When the body is too warm, it triggers sweating and widens blood vessels in the skin. When the body is too cold, it triggers shivering and narrows blood vessels in the skin. Each response pushes temperature back toward the set point.

Two pieces of physics make it work. Evaporation: when sweat turns from liquid to vapor, it takes heat with it, cooling the skin. Blood flow: wide skin vessels bring warm blood near the surface, where its heat escapes to the air; narrow vessels keep warm blood deep in the body. Shivering is fast, small muscle contractions, and working muscles release heat from cellular respiration.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: When the body is too cold: shivering and narrowed skin blood vessels.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Blood vessels reach every part of the skin, which is how they can carry heat to the surface or keep it in.

blocks.title: A hot day
blocks.q: A runner's temperature rises during a race on a hot day. Describe the feedback loop.
steps: Stimulus: temperature rises above the set point.
Sensors in the skin and brain detect it; the hypothalamus responds.
Effectors: sweat glands release sweat and skin vessels widen.
Sweat evaporates and warm blood near the skin loses heat.
blocks.a: Temperature falls back toward 37 °C: negative feedback.

blocks.title: Why humid days feel worse
blocks.q: On a very humid day, sweat drips off instead of drying. Why does the body cool less?
steps: Cooling comes from evaporation.
Humid air already holds a lot of water vapor, so sweat evaporates slowly.
blocks.a: Less evaporation carries away less heat.

blocks.html: Other animals use the same ideas in different ways. Dogs pant, which evaporates water from the mouth and tongue. Elephants flap their large ears, which are full of blood vessels. Lizards and snakes, which get most of their heat from their surroundings, control their temperature mainly by behavior: moving into the sun or into shade.

It seems natural to think sweat cools you because it is cold. Sweat comes out at about body temperature. It cools the skin as it evaporates, because turning liquid water into vapor takes heat, and that heat comes from your skin.

blocks.html: Cells burn glucose in cellular respiration, so they need a steady supply. But you eat only a few times a day. Two hormones from the pancreas keep the blood's glucose level steady between and after meals, a pair of negative feedback loops.

After a meal, blood glucose rises, and the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin helps body cells take up glucose and tells the liver to store it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls. Between meals, blood glucose falls, and the pancreas releases glucagon, which tells the liver to break glycogen down and release glucose, so blood glucose rises.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Switch between high and low blood glucose: insulin lowers it; glucagon raises it.

blocks.html: Why two hormones instead of one? With one signal you could only push in one direction. Two opposing signals let the body correct both a rise and a fall, like having both a furnace and an air conditioner. Clusters of cells in the pancreas (islets) do the sensing: beta cells make insulin and alpha cells make glucagon.

blocks.name: bi-chart
blocks.cap: An example of the pattern after a meal: glucose rises, insulin follows, and both settle back.

blocks.title: After a meal
blocks.q: An hour after lunch, which hormone is high, and what does the liver do?
steps: Blood glucose has risen from digested food.
The pancreas releases insulin.
Insulin signals the liver to take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
blocks.a: Insulin is high; the liver stores glucose as glycogen.

blocks.title: During a long hike
blocks.q: Hours after breakfast, a hiker's blood glucose starts to fall. What keeps it from falling too far?
steps: The pancreas senses the drop and releases glucagon.
Glucagon tells the liver to break glycogen down into glucose and release it.
blocks.a: Glucagon and the liver's glycogen store.

blocks.html: The liver is the body's glucose bank. Glycogen, the stored form, is a branched chain of many glucose units (see Carbohydrates), so it can be built up quickly after a meal and broken down quickly when glucose runs low. Muscles store glycogen too, but they keep it for their own use.

Two common confusions: thinking insulin is a kind of sugar, and thinking both hormones push the same way. Insulin is a protein hormone that lowers blood glucose; glucagon is another protein hormone that raises it. Check: "insulin in, sugar in (to cells)"; glucagon makes the liver let glucose "go".

blocks.html: You met the organ systems one at a time in How Body Systems Work Together. In high school biology the focus is on how they work together to keep up homeostasis.
The body is organized in levels: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and the systems together make the organism. Most jobs need several systems at once.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Switch between systems. Each has its own organs, but none works alone.

blocks.html: Each level can do something the level below cannot. One muscle cell can contract, but only a muscle (an organ, with muscle, nerve and connective tissue) can move a bone, and only the muscular and skeletal systems together can carry you up a flight of stairs. Specialization makes each part good at one job, which makes every part depend on the others.

blocks.title: Oxygen for a running leg
blocks.q: Which systems work together to get oxygen to the muscles of a runner's legs?
steps: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the lungs.
The circulatory system carries it in the blood to the leg muscles.
The nervous and endocrine systems speed up breathing and heart rate.
blocks.a: Respiratory, circulatory, nervous and endocrine systems, at least.

blocks.title: Getting rid of carbon dioxide
blocks.q: Muscle cells make carbon dioxide in cellular respiration. Which systems remove it from the body?
steps: The circulatory system carries it in the blood to the lungs.
The respiratory system breathes it out.

items: Digestive and circulatory: nutrients absorbed in the small intestine travel in the blood to every cell.
Nervous and muscular: nerves signal muscles to contract.
Excretory and circulatory: the kidneys filter wastes out of the blood.
Endocrine and the rest: hormones carried in the blood coordinate many organs at once.

blocks.html: It is common to describe each system as if it worked alone. Almost every function needs several. Ask of any process: what brings the materials, what carries them, what controls it, and what removes the wastes? Usually that is three or four systems.

blocks.html: The circulatory system, part of the team of body systems, is the body's delivery route. The heart is really two pumps side by side, each sending blood around its own loop.

Blood makes two loops. The right side of the heart pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs (the pulmonary loop). Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left side, which pumps it to the body (the systemic loop), and it comes back to the right side. Valves keep blood moving one way.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Step along the path: body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.

blocks.html: Why two loops? The lungs' capillaries are delicate and need gentle pressure, while blood sent to the whole body needs strong pressure to reach the toes and back. Two separate pumps let each loop run at its own pressure. That is also why the left ventricle has the thickest wall: it does the hardest pumping.

items: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back to the heart; capillaries, one cell thick, connect them and exchange materials with the tissues.
The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs; the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood back.
The aorta, the largest artery, carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body.

blocks.title: One trip around
blocks.q: A red blood cell is in the right atrium. List, in order, where it goes until it reaches the aorta.
steps: Right atrium → right ventricle.
Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
blocks.a: Right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta.

blocks.title: How many times through the heart?
blocks.q: On one complete trip from the toes back to the toes, how many times does a blood cell pass through the heart?
steps: Once through the right side, on the way to the lungs.
Once through the left side, on the way back to the body.

blocks.html: Two errors are common. One is picturing one loop: heart → lungs → body → heart. The blood comes back to the heart between the lungs and the body. The other is thinking every artery carries oxygen-rich blood. Arteries are defined by direction, away from the heart: the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

blocks.html: The pulmonary loop brings oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. There, gases cross by simple diffusion, down their concentration gradients.

In the alveoli, tiny air sacs at the ends of the airways, oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air. Huge surface area, very thin walls and steady blood flow and breathing keep the gradients steep and the exchange fast.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Step along the path of air: nose, trachea, then the lungs, where it reaches the alveoli.

blocks.html: Diffusion is fastest when the distance is short, the area is large and the difference in concentration is big. The lungs maximize all three. An adult's lungs hold about 300 million alveoli with a combined surface of about 70 square meters, and the wall between air and blood is only about two cells thick. Breathing keeps bringing fresh, oxygen-rich air, and blood flow keeps carrying oxygen away, so the gradient never runs down.

blocks.name: bi-membrane
blocks.cap: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, with no pump.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: Air in an alveolus has a high level of oxygen and a low level of carbon dioxide. Blood arriving in the lung capillary has low oxygen and high carbon dioxide. Which way does each gas move?
steps: Each gas diffuses from where it is higher to where it is lower.
Oxygen: higher in the air, so into the blood.
Carbon dioxide: higher in the blood, so into the air.
blocks.a: Oxygen into the blood; carbon dioxide into the alveolus, to be breathed out.

blocks.title: Why it keeps going
blocks.q: If blood stopped flowing past an alveolus, what would happen to oxygen diffusion there?
steps: The blood would fill with oxygen until it matched the air.
With no difference left, net diffusion stops.
blocks.a: It would stop, because the gradient would disappear.

blocks.html: At the other end of the trip, in the tissues, the gradients run the opposite way: cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, so oxygen diffuses out of the blood into the cells, and carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood.

It is natural to picture the lungs pumping oxygen into the blood. No pump moves the gases across. Gas exchange is passive diffusion down concentration gradients. What breathing and blood flow do is keep those gradients steep.

blocks.html: Food arrives as large molecules: starch, proteins and fats (see Monomers and Polymers). They are too big to cross the gut wall. Enzymes break them into small units by hydrolysis, and the small intestine absorbs them.

Each digestive enzyme fits its own substrate. Amylase splits starch into sugars. Proteases (such as pepsin and trypsin) split proteins into amino acids. Lipase splits fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Villi, finger-like folds lining the small intestine, absorb the products into the blood, and fats into the lymph.

blocks.name: bi-enzyme
blocks.cap: Each enzyme has its own best pH: pepsin works in the acid of the stomach, trypsin in the mildly basic small intestine.

blocks.html: Why so many enzymes? An enzyme works because its active site fits one kind of substrate (the lock-and-key idea). The bond that holds sugars together in starch is not the bond that holds amino acids together in a protein, so one enzyme cannot cut both. And each part of the gut has its own pH, so each enzyme is built to work at the pH where it acts.

blocks.title: Following a cracker
blocks.q: Where does the starch in a cracker start being digested, and where is it finished and absorbed?
steps: Salivary amylase starts splitting starch in the mouth.
Stomach acid stops salivary amylase.
Pancreatic amylase and enzymes on the intestine wall finish the job in the small intestine, where the sugars are absorbed by the villi.
blocks.a: It starts in the mouth and is finished and absorbed in the small intestine.

blocks.html: Bile, made by the liver, is not an enzyme. It breaks fat into tiny droplets (emulsifies it), giving lipase much more surface to work on. The large intestine absorbs water, and bacteria living there make some vitamins.

It is easy to think one enzyme digests all foods. Each enzyme fits particular substrates, and each part of the gut has its own pH and its own enzymes. Pepsin, for example, works in the stomach's acid and stops working in the small intestine.

blocks.html: The nervous system, one member of the team of body systems, carries fast signals. Its cells, the neurons, use the ion channels and pumps you studied in membranes to send electrical messages.

A neuron receives signals at its dendrites, and sends an electrical impulse, the action potential, from the cell body along its axon. At the axon's end, the synapse, it releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, which cross a tiny gap and signal the next cell.

A resting neuron is charged like a tiny battery: the sodium-potassium pump keeps more sodium outside and more potassium inside, so the inside sits at about −70 millivolts. When a signal is strong enough, sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, flipping the voltage; then potassium channels open and potassium flows out, resetting it. That flip triggers the next patch of membrane, so the impulse travels down the axon like a wave in a stadium.

blocks.cap: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; nerves carry signals to and from the rest of the body.

blocks.title: Signal speed
blocks.q: A nerve impulse travels 1.2 meters from the spinal cord to a toe in 0.02 seconds. How fast is it?
steps: Speed = distance ÷ time.

blocks.title: Direction
blocks.q: Why does a signal cross a synapse in only one direction?
steps: Only the axon ending releases neurotransmitters.
Only the next cell has the receptors that bind them.
blocks.a: Release happens on one side and reception on the other.

blocks.html: Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty layer that lets the impulse jump between gaps and travel much faster: from about 1 meter per second in thin, bare axons to more than 100 meters per second in thick, myelinated ones. A reflex, like pulling a hand from something hot, uses a short path through the spinal cord, so it happens before the brain even notices.

It is natural to picture the electrical signal jumping straight from one neuron to the next. At most synapses it does not. The electrical signal is turned into a chemical one: neurotransmitters cross the gap, and the next cell starts its own electrical signal.

blocks.html: You met the body's defenses in The Body's Defenses. They work in two layers, which differ in speed and in aim. This topic builds on the teamwork of body systems: immune cells travel in the blood and lymph.

Innate defenses act fast against anything foreign: skin and mucus, inflammation, and white blood cells such as macrophages that engulf germs. Adaptive defenses take days the first time but target one particular invader: B cells make antibodies, and T cells destroy infected cells and direct the response. Adaptive defenses leave memory cells, so a second encounter brings a faster, stronger response.

Why two layers? Innate defenses are ready at once but cannot tell one germ from another. Adaptive defenses take time because the body must find, among millions of B and T cells with different receptors, the few that fit this invader, and then multiply them. That search is slow the first time. Afterward, some of those cells stay as memory cells, so the search is already done.

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: Lymph nodes, the spleen and other immune organs, where white blood cells gather and meet invaders.

blocks.title: Innate or adaptive?
blocks.q: A macrophage engulfs bacteria that entered a scraped knee, within hours. Which defense is this?
steps: It acts quickly.
It attacks bacteria in general, not one particular kind.

blocks.title: Reading the response
blocks.q: In the chart, how many days after each exposure does the antibody level peak?
steps: First exposure (day 0): the peak is at day 14, so 14 days.
Second exposure (day 35): the peak is at day 49, also 14 days later, but about eight times higher; and antibodies are already rising by day 42.
blocks.a: Both about 14 days, but the second response rises sooner and much higher.

blocks.html: Vaccines work by this memory. In the CDC's words, "vaccines help develop immunity by imitating an infection": they show the immune system a harmless form or part of a germ, so memory cells form without the illness. Antibiotics are a different tool: they act on bacteria and do not work on viruses.

Two misunderstandings are common. Antibodies are not cells; they are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells, which bind to one particular invader. And the immune system does not forget every invader: memory cells make a second response faster and stronger.

blocks.html: Cells make wastes, and the amount of water and salt in the blood has to stay in a narrow range. The kidneys handle both. They depend on osmosis and are part of the team of body systems, working closely with the circulatory system.

Each kidney has about a million filtering units called nephrons. A nephron filters water and small molecules out of the blood, reabsorbs what the body needs (most of the water, glucose, many salts), and leaves the wastes, such as urea, in the urine. The hormone ADH makes the kidneys keep more water when the body is short of it.

Why filter almost everything and then take most of it back? Filtering by size is simple and catches every small waste, even ones the body has never met. Then the tubule can be choosy, returning only what is useful. The numbers are striking: the kidneys filter about 150 quarts of blood a day, and only 1 to 2 quarts become urine (NIDDK).

blocks.name: bi-body
blocks.cap: The kidneys, the ureters and the bladder.

blocks.name: bi-feedback
blocks.cap: Water balance: when the blood is short of water, more ADH reaches the kidneys, which keep more water.

blocks.title: How much is reabsorbed?
blocks.q: Suppose a person's kidneys filter 180 liters of fluid in a day and 1.8 liters leave as urine. What percent of the filtered fluid was reabsorbed?
steps: Reabsorbed: 180 − 1.8 = 178.2 liters.

blocks.title: A hot day without water
blocks.q: After hours outdoors with nothing to drink, what happens to ADH and to the urine?
steps: The blood is short of water, so the brain releases more ADH.
ADH makes the nephrons reabsorb more water.
blocks.a: ADH rises, and the urine is smaller in amount and darker (more concentrated).

blocks.html: Glucose is filtered too, but healthy kidneys reabsorb all of it, so normally none is in the urine. The kidneys also help control salt levels, blood pressure and the blood's pH.

It is natural to think the kidneys pick out only the harmful things. They filter almost everything small out of the blood, useful or not, and then take back what the body needs. Check with glucose: it leaves the blood in the filter and returns in the tubule.

blocks.html: Plants keep their insides steady too. A leaf needs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, but every opening that lets carbon dioxide in also lets water vapor out. Water moving up from the roots cannot always keep up, so plants use osmosis to control their leaf pores, in a feedback loop.

Stomata are pores in the leaf, each between two guard cells. When water is plentiful, guard cells swell (become turgid) and bow apart, opening the pore. When water is short, they go limp and the pore closes. This balances carbon dioxide intake against water loss.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Drag the water slider: guard cells swell and open the pore when water is plentiful, and close it when water is short.

blocks.html: Guard cells open by osmosis. In light, with water available, they pump in potassium ions; water follows by osmosis, the cells swell, and because their inner walls are thicker, they bend apart. In a drought, the hormone abscisic acid (ABA) signals the guard cells to let potassium out; water leaves, the cells go slack and the pore shuts. Less water lost is the response that reverses the problem: negative feedback.

blocks.title: A dry afternoon
blocks.q: On a hot, dry afternoon, a plant's soil is drying out. What happens to its stomata, and what does that cost?
steps: Water is short, so ABA builds up and guard cells lose water.
The stomata close, saving water.
But carbon dioxide can no longer get in.
blocks.a: The stomata close; the plant saves water but photosynthesis slows.

blocks.title: Where are the stomata?
blocks.q: Many plants have more stomata on the underside of their leaves. Why might that help?
steps: The underside is shaded and cooler.
Less water evaporates there.
blocks.a: It lets carbon dioxide in while losing less water.

blocks.name: bi-plant
blocks.cap: Water moves up the xylem and out through the stomata (transpiration); sugar moves down the phloem.

blocks.html: Plants in dry places have other ways to save water: thick waxy coatings, fewer stomata, and, in plants such as cactuses, opening stomata only at night, when it is cooler, and storing the carbon dioxide until daytime.

Stomata are often described as holes that let oxygen out. They are mainly a trade-off: open, they let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis, and they also let water vapor out. Oxygen does leave through them, but controlling water loss is why the plant opens and closes them.
